name: Ivan Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Ivan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and what you say is confidential. So you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Aldous Penhale at Top Carrow. It's hill sheep, about six hundred Swaledale ewes, and forty acres of spring barley lower down. Aldous is 71 and a widower with no children, and he's teaching me the place, slowly, because I've a lot to learn. Today I was gathering the hill with the dogs, and my dog Moss did more work than I did.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is there a plan for the farm, between you and Aldous?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nothing on paper. He's said, more than once, that if I stick at it he'd sooner the farm went to someone who'll work it than to a stranger. That's what keeps me here on the bottom wage, with about three weeks' money saved and a flat above the post office in Carrow. In summer I go shearing for other farms to make a bit extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to work. I'd probably say it at the auction mart, someone would agree, someone would argue. I'm not one for posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. My future is the farm and Aldous, not computers. If nothing big changes, I've got years to learn the place and maybe take it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, work hard, learn from Aldous. I'd do more shearing in summer, try to save a bit more. Maybe ask Aldous about putting something on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. My mate Rhys showed me, I ask it about the weather for gathering, or what a lamb's symptoms might mean before I ring the vet. It's handy, but I'd not trust it over Aldous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn from Aldous in the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. Which bit of the hill floods, which ewes to keep, how to price lambs at the mart. Aldous knows things nobody wrote down, and he's not getting younger.

S0.say: Good, now we can get back to work. I'd say it at the auction mart, where some would agree and some would argue.
S0.think: It suits me, because my future is the farm and Aldous, not computers. If nothing changes, I've got years to learn the place and maybe take it on.
S0.do: Keeps working and learning from Aldous, and takes on more summer shearing to save more. May ask Aldous to put the succession plan on paper.
S0.quote: Aldous knows things nobody wrote down, and he's not getting younger.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan's whole future is tied to an informal promise from Aldous, which makes him patient about low pay. He uses AI for small questions but trusts Aldous more. Shearing gives him a second income in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have every right to use whatever works, that's how farming's always moved on. I'd say if you're willing to work and learn, there'll be a place for you. I don't want the government stopping it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd make me uneasy. Hill farming is slower to change, but the barley, the feeding, maybe even gathering with drones, could all go. But if I take the farm on, I'd be the one choosing the robots, not the one replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI a bit more, to get on top of the farm accounts and the grants. I'd look at a short course on farm machinery, once I'd seen the robots working on another farm. And I'd push Aldous to put the farm plan on paper, because a promise isn't much in a changing world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I had a direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Aldous take on new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. He'd say no at first. Then he'd see the neighbour's drone gather a hill in an hour and he'd ask me to look into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your shearing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more of a worry. There are shearing machines being tested, and if they work, my summer money goes. I'd keep doing it as long as farmers wanted a person.

S1.say: Farmers have every right to use whatever works, that's how farming has always moved on. If you're willing to work and learn, there'll be a place for you, and the government shouldn't stop it.
S1.think: It'd make me uneasy, because the barley, the feeding and even gathering could change. But if I take the farm on, I'd be the one choosing the robots, not the one replaced.
S1.do: Uses AI more for farm accounts and grants and takes a short machinery course once he's seen robots working on another farm. Pushes Aldous to put the succession plan on paper.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but with a sense of direction.
S1.quote: I'd be the one choosing the robots, not the one replaced.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan supports farmers' freedom to bring in machines and sees himself as a future owner, not just a worker. His steady nature shows in waiting to see robots working elsewhere first. His shearing income is the part he feels most exposed on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people will find a way, they always do. I'd say families and communities need to stick together. I'd not want the government taking over everything because of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. If robots can run the hill, Aldous could sell to some company that runs a hundred farms with no people. My whole plan is a promise from an old man, and in two years that might be worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Aldous straight away and ask him straight what he means to do. I'd cut back on everything, stop the car payment, sell my second dog. I'd take any extra work going, shearing, fencing, anything. If it went wrong, I'd go back to my parents' farm cottage for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AGI can run a farm, what happens to your hope of taking on Top Carrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It depends on Aldous. If he still wants a person, the farm still needs an owner, even if robots do the work. But someone with money might offer him more than I could ever pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car first, I'd get by on the quad and lifts. Then the extras, the pub, the football. I'd keep the dogs, Moss at least, she's family.

S2.say: It's a shock, but people will find a way, they always do. Families and communities need to stick together, and the government shouldn't take over everything because of it.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, because if robots can run the hill, Aldous could sell to a company that runs a hundred farms with no people. My whole plan is a promise from an old man, and in two years that might be worth nothing.
S2.do: Asks Aldous directly about his plans for the farm and cuts back, giving up his car payment and second dog. Takes any extra work going and moves back to his parents' cottage if needed.
S2.quote: My whole plan is a promise from an old man, and in two years that might be worth nothing.
S2.fieldNote: Two years exposes how fragile Ivan's future is: everything rests on an unwritten promise. His free-market outlook stays, but he fears outside money buying the farm. He'd act by asking Aldous straight and cutting back, with his parents as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so let's not panic. I'd tell young farmers to learn the business side, not just the work. And I'd say keep farms in families and local hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to get the farm plan on paper. If I own a share by then, robots could even help me run it. If I don't, I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get Aldous to see a solicitor and write down the plan. I'd do a farm business course at the college in winter, and use the AI to learn the grants and paperwork. I'd save hard from shearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a job to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years do for the plan with Aldous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it urgent. Two years was too fast to do anything. Five years is time to sort a will, maybe a share in the farm. That's what I'd push for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you work the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a few things once they'd proven themselves, like drones for gathering. I'd want to be the one deciding, not waiting for it to happen to me.

S3.say: We've got time to get ready, so let's not panic. Young farmers should learn the business side, not just the work, and farms should stay in families and local hands.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get the farm plan on paper. If I own a share by then, robots could even help me run it, and if I don't, I'm in trouble.
S3.do: Gets Aldous to see a solicitor and put the succession plan in writing, and takes a winter farm business course at the college. Uses AI to learn grants and paperwork and saves hard from shearing.
S3.feel: Anxious but focused on a task.
S3.quote: If I own a share by then, robots could even help me run it. If I don't, I'm in trouble.
S3.fieldNote: For Ivan, five years is about securing ownership. The scenario turns his hope into a list: a solicitor, a will, a business course. He'd adopt drones once proven, as long as he's the one deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's time to do it right. I'd say keep working, keep learning, and keep the land in good hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd probably be all right, if the plan with Aldous goes through. It's the same end point, but I'd be an owner by then, maybe with a robot or two. That's a different place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, the solicitor, the business course, the shearing. Over the next few years, buy into the farm a bit at a time with what I save. I'd take up machines once I'd seen them work elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts Aldous at 81. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, he might not be here. That's the hard part. Ten years means the farm decision happens before AGI, not after, which is better for me, but I'd miss him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for yourself, beyond the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wife, a family, kids who grow up on the hill. That's what I'd want. Ten years means there's time for that.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, there's time to do it right. Keep working, keep learning and keep the land in good hands.
S4.think: I'd probably be all right if the plan with Aldous goes through. It's the same end point, but I'd be an owner by then, maybe with a robot or two, and that's a different place to be.
S4.do: Sees the solicitor, takes the business course and keeps shearing in the first year. Buys into the farm bit by bit with savings and takes up machines once proven elsewhere.
S4.quote: Ten years means the farm decision happens before AGI, not after, which is better for me, but I'd miss him.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years means the farm's future is settled before AGI, which steadies Ivan. He's honest that this depends on Aldous's age, and is clearly fond of him. He pictures a family on the hill and owning the robots rather than being replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the farm could be sold before I'd had a chance. What would help is help for young people to buy into farms, cheap loans or tax breaks for passing farms on to workers, and apprenticeships. Not handouts, a way in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the land, in the end. If it's all big companies with robots, the hills will be worked but nobody will live there. I'd rather be poor and on the hill than comfortable in a town.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be poor and on the hill than comfortable in a town.
portrait: Ivan Haddad is 27 and works on Top Carrow, a hill sheep and barley farm owned by Aldous Penhale, a 71-year-old widower with no children who has hinted the farm could pass to Ivan. He lives above the post office in Carrow, earns extra shearing in summer and has about three weeks of savings. He backs farmers' freedom to use machines and wants apprenticeships, not handouts. He is calm in the plateau, uneasy with steady disruption, and alarmed by AGI in two years because his future rests on an unwritten promise. With more warning time he would get the succession plan written down, study the business side and buy into the farm bit by bit.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the farm could be sold to an outside company before he had a chance to buy in.
whatWouldHelp: Help for young people to buy into farms, such as cheap loans or tax breaks for passing farms to workers, plus apprenticeships rather than handouts.
